chapter.title: Tutorial: Creation of input files
chapter.para: Here you can find a detailed description how input files for the catflow wizard are made from the digital elevation model (DEM).

section.title: Creating the grid (tin) of your digital elevation model DEM
section.para: Depending on the format of your DEM data, there are different ways to generate a grid. Check the ArcToolbox Conversion Tools for an import filter for your data. The DEM as shown in figure will be used throughout this tutorial.
At the university of Oslo, there is a exercise to convert contour lines into a DEM. The corresponding text is also here:

The first approach is to create a TIN from the contours, and then interpolate a grid. You use three coverages, (1) contour lines, (2) river lines, (3) lakes. Contour lines contain your information about altitudes, rivers are break lines indicating local minimums in the terrain, and lakes are pits, indicating a flat area with constant altitude. You create the dataset with the command "ARCTIN", consult the tutor about syntax. You can also start the ARCTOOLS program which gives you a more menu-based approach (use "command tools"->"conversion"->"surface"->"tin builder". The resulting TIN must be converted into a grid by the command "TINLATTICE". Here you have the choice between a linear and a spline (quintic) interpolator, check and assess both results.

This can also be done in ArcGIS. Here you display your data sets first (contours, rivers, lakes). From the 3D analyst toolbar you make the TIN from selected coverages. This is the user-friendly option. In both cases you should introduce break lines also for ridges. These break lines you must digitise manually on the screen (make a new data set, lines, digitze lines on areas indicating large transitions of topography, such as steep mountain walls). We will help you with this during the lab.

The second approach is to use the TOPOGRID-algorithm in ArcInfo. This is based on an algorithm proposed by Hutchinson (1989). Open Arc (ArcGIS->ArcInfo Workstation>Arc), go to your workspace and try the command "topogridtool". This is a window based interface to topogrid, but you might need to get some help from the tutor here as well. The interpolator is a local spline, iteratively adapting an elevation model to the data points. You can read more about this in the ArcDoc or :

section.title: Activate the hydrology sample extension
section.para: This tutorial was writen based on ESRI Hydrotools Version 2 (Distributed with ArcMap 8.3, Build 800). You need administrators rights to activate the hydrology extension!

listitem.para: Open the Tools:Customize dialog from the menu
Click on Add from Files...
Select C:\arcgis\arcexe83\ArcObjects Developer Kit\Samples\Spatial Analyst\Hydrology Modeling\esrihydrology_v2.dll and click on Open
Activate the Hydrology Modeling Toolbar and click on Close

section.title: Vectorized river network
section.para: Once your DEM is available as grid or tin the hydrology extension may be used to generate a vectorized river network. Note that the hydrology extension is based on the spatial-analyst. You can define the extent of your analysis to some part of your DEM (e.g. the catchment boundaries) using the spatial-analysts option menu from the toolbar (see activateToolbars for activating the corresponding toolbar) as shown here:

If you have a river network available as a shape file (vector) it is probably based on additional information besides the DEM. Consider to use this version or a mixed version of a river network instead of generating a version only based on the DEM.
Sample DEM: Malalcahuello, Chile
The following steps are necessary to create the vectorized river network

listitem.para: Create a depressionless DEM as described in the corresponding chapter of the hydrology extension manual.
Create a flow direction file as describe in the corresponding chapter of the hydrology extension manual.
Create a flow accumulation file as describe in the corresponding chapter of the hydrology extension manual.

Create a river net shape file as describe in the corresponding chapter of the hydrology extension manual. In "Präprozessing für das Programm CATFLOW" (Casper, Lindenmaier, Maurer und Zehe, 2003) the minimum number of cells for a stream is suggested to be 100. However, this value may be altered according to your needs.
Since a shapefile for the river network in Malalcahuello existed before, that version will be used for the rest of this tutorial instead of the network derived from the DEM.

section.title: Slope delineation
section.para:
Before creating the slope delineation, make sure the following three toolbars are active: Editor, Spatial Analyst and Topology.
Activating Toolbars

listitem.para: In ArcCatalog copy (edit:copy and edit:paste) your shapefile with the vectorized river network into a new file called borders.shp.
Create a new polygon shape files (File:New...:Shape...) in ArcCatalog called hillslope. As Spatial Reference, import the coordinate system from your river network shape file (Edit...:Import...).
Add the two new shapefiles (borders and hillslope) to your view in ArcMap (File:Add data...).
Delineate your overall catchment as described in

Convert your overall catchment into a polygon using the spatial analyst (Spatial Analyst:Convert:RasterToFeatures...). Use the catchment created in the previous step as your input raster. Use a polygon for the output feature and call the resulting theme catchborder.
Start an editing session in your shapefile borders (Editor:Start edititing).

In the editor toolbar, set the task to Create New Feature and the target to borders. Using the selectFeature tool, select the catchment border polygon from catchborder.
Click on constructFeatures on the topology tool bar to add the catchment boundary to the borders shape file.
Display the borders theme together with your flow direction raster. This will be your base to digitize your hill slopes.
Set the snap environment (Editor:Snapping...) to the Edges and Vertezes of the borders theme.

Use the sketch tool to digitize the hillslopes based on the direction raster. As a general rule, points of the same hillslope share the same flow direction. You can also use the rain drop tool to determine the local flow direction. Also make sure, hillslopes have unique soil and land use properties.

In the editor toolbar, set the target to your hillslope theme. Using the selectFeature tool, select all lines from your borders theme. Click on constructFeatures on the topology tool bar to add the just defined hill slopes to the hillslope shape file.

In ArcMap Version "8.3 Build 800" a bug causes the created polygons to have errors (a part of the points are shifted). This error does not occur if the catchment border from the catchborder theme is copied into the hillslope theme.

If lines in your river network are not snaped correctly, some of your hillslopes are connected. This does not happen if your river net is build with the hydro sample extension as described in . To snap your river network correctly, use the clean command in arcInfo workstation.
End your edit session and save changes Editor: Stop Editing theme. Hillslope.shp contains your hillslope features.
Display the attribute table of your hillslope theme. Add a new integer field to contain the ID.
Right click on the heading of the new column and click Calculate Values. You must confirm the following question.
Calculate the slope ID to be equal to the FID, the ArcGis object ID.

section.title: Slope lines
section.note: Note that the wizard will check the direction of your slope lines. If the outlet is higher than the start point of your slope line (heights from your DEM), the line is flipped. Make sure that your DEM has differing heights for start point and outlet of your slope line.

listitem.para: Create a new line shape files (File:New...:Shape...) in ArcCatalog called slopeLines. As Spatial Reference, import the coordinate system from your river network shape file (Edit...:Import...).
Add the new shapefile to your view in ArcMap (File:Add data...).
start an editing session with your shapefile slopeLines (Editor:Start edititing).
Display the hillSlope and the river network theme. This will be your base to digitize your slope lines.
Set the snap environment (Editor:Snapping...) to the Edges and Vertezes of the river theme.

In the editor toolbar, set the task to Create New Feature and the target to slopeLines. Use the sketch tool to digitize the slope lines. You can also use the rain drop tool to determine the local flow direction.
End your edit session and save changes Editor: Stop Editing theme. slopelines.shp contains your slope line features.

Right click on your slope line layer in the table of contents and click Joins and Relates:Join.... Join the data based on the geographical location with the hillslope theme. Each line will be given the attributes if it falls completely inside a polygon. Save the new theme as lineID. This theme contains the slope line features with the same IDs as the hillslopes.
